passages.title: A mocker demands the coming punishment
passages.tafsir:
This passage opens Surah al-Ma'arij ("The Ways of Ascent") with a real taunt: a disbeliever, mocking the Prophet's ﷺ warning, demands that Allah's promised punishment simply happen already — daring Him to bring it on. Ayat 1–4 answer that dare not by describing the punishment itself but by establishing three unshakeable facts about it: it is coming (*waqi'*), it cannot be turned back, and it comes from a Being who owns the very stairways to the highest heights of creation (*dhul-ma'arij*) — whose court convenes on a Day so vast that its own measure is fifty thousand years, the very Day on which the angels ascend to Him.

## Who Asked, and Why

Two threads in the sources converge on who this "sa'il" (demander) was. Maarif ul-Qur'an, citing a narration An-Nasa'i transmits from Ibn 'Abbas, names him: Nadr ibn al-Harith, who in openly rejecting the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ cried out the very words the Qur'an elsewhere records: "O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from you, then rain down stones on us from the sky or bring on us a painful torment" (8:32). Maarif adds the outcome, citing Mazhari's report from Ibn Abi Hatim: Nadr ibn al-Harith was later killed by the Muslims at the Battle of Badr.

Ibn Kathir preserves the same link from another angle. Mujahid explained the sa'il this way: "A person called out (requesting) for the torment that will occur in the Hereafter to happen" — and identified that very demand with the words of 8:32. Al-'Awfi's report from Ibn 'Abbas gives the wider frame: "That is the questioning of the disbelievers about the torment of Allah and it will occur to them." Maarif ul-Qur'an's introduction to the surah paints the same scene: the disbelievers would come to the Prophet ﷺ in groups, mocking the Muslims and denying the Resurrection, while ironically claiming — as a jeer — that they themselves expected to enter Paradise anyway.

## A Demand, Not a Question

Maarif ul-Qur'an draws out something the English can't fully carry: the Arabic *su'al* (to ask) works two ways. Followed by the preposition *'an* ("about"), it means a genuine inquiry. Followed by *bi* ("for" — as here, *sa'ala sa'ilun bi-'adhab*), it means a request, a demand for something to be produced. This *sa'il* was not asking whether the punishment was real; he was daring Allah to bring it, exactly as in 8:32. Ibn Kathir makes the same point grammatically: the letter *Ba* carries an assumed sense of hastening — the man was demanding the punishment he denied, not sincerely inquiring about it. Ibn Kathir places this beside a near-identical Qur'anic scene: "And they ask you to hasten on the torment! And Allah fails not His promise" (22:47) — the same mockery, met with the same assurance that it will occur and cannot be avoided.

## "Bound to Come," None Can Avert It

*Waqi'* — translated "bound to come" — Ibn 'Abbas glossed it simply: "*Waqi'* means coming." Ibn Kathir explains that the word means the punishment "is waiting in preparation for the disbelievers." Maarif ul-Qur'an adds that the punishment "is inevitable and will most certainly occur in this world or in the Hereafter or in both the worlds" — it cannot be averted.

Ayah 2 then closes off any hope of escape: *laysa lahu dafi'* — "there is no one who can repel it," as Ibn Kathir puts it, "if Allah wants it to happen."

## "Lord of the Ways of Ascent"

Ayah 3 grounds that certainty in who issues the decree: Allah, *dhul-ma'arij* — "Lord of the ways of ascent." Maarif ul-Qur'an explains *ma'arij* as the plural of *mi'raj*, a ladder or staircase with steps for reaching high places. As a description of Allah, the scholars read it two ways. Sa'id ibn Jubair (per Maarif) took it as "Lord of high degrees" — a statement of Allah's own loftiness; Ibn 'Abbas, in the report Ibn Kathir preserves through Ali ibn Abi Talhah, likewise reads it as "loftiness and abundance." Others read it more concretely: Mujahid said it means "the ways of ascension into the heavens," and Ibn Mas'ud (per Maarif) specified these ascending stairways as the seven heavens stacked one above another, so that *dhul-ma'arij* effectively means "Lord of the heavens" (*malik us-samawat*).

Maarif ul-Qur'an points out why this title sits exactly here: it is, in its own words, "the proof of the preceding statement" — the punishment comes "from the Lord of the Ascending Steps," and so "it is not possible for anyone to avert it."

## A Day of Fifty Thousand Years

Ayah 4 describes the angels and "the Ruh" ascending to Allah on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years. Multiple early authorities — Ibn 'Abbas (through what Ibn Kathir calls an authentic chain), Ikrimah, Ad-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd — agree this Day is the Day of Judgement itself. Ibn 'Abbas's fuller wording matters: this is the measure of the Day "for the disbelievers" specifically — a phrase that opens the door to everything Maarif ul-Qur'an builds on it below.

On *ta'ruju* ("ascend"), Qatadah's gloss is simply "to ascend." On "the Ruh," Ibn Kathir records two possibilities: Abu Salih described the Ruh as creatures resembling humans, part of Allah's creation, but not human; alternatively, "the Ruh" here may specifically mean Jibril, named separately from "the angels" as a mark of his special honor — the same point Maarif ul-Qur'an makes for this ayah — or it may name the souls (*arwah*) of the children of Adam, which are lifted to the heavens at death, a point the sources say a hadith concerning al-Bara' supports.

### How Long Is the Day, Really?

This is where Maarif ul-Qur'an goes deepest on this passage, because a real question arises: elsewhere the Qur'an (32:5) describes a Day whose measure is a *thousand* years, not fifty thousand. Maarif resolves this using two hadiths cited by Mazhari. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrates that the Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ about the length of this Day, and he swore: "I swear by the Being in Whose control is my life! The day for the believers will be lighter and less than the time during which they would perform an obligatory salah" (transmitted, per Mazhari, by Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Hibban, and al-Bayhaqi, through a chain using "'an"). A second report from Abu Hurayrah — conveyed both as a statement of the Prophet ﷺ and as his own words, per Mazhari, and reported by al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi — says the Day, for the believers, will feel like the time between 'Asr and Maghrib.

Maarif's conclusion: length and shortness on that Day are relative, not fixed. For the die-hard disbelievers it is truly fifty thousand years; for sincere believers it collapses to something shorter than a single prayer, or the span between two afternoon prayers; some disbelieving groups in between may experience something closer to the thousand years of 32:5. Mazhari also offers a second, complementary reading of the Sajdah verse: that it may describe an actual physical day of this world — the angels' round trip between heaven and earth, each leg of which authentic hadiths describe as a five-hundred-year journey for a human traveler, totaling a thousand years — while the fifty-thousand-year Day of ayah 4 here is specifically the Day of Judgement, a different reckoning altogether. Maarif closes simply: "Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best."

## From the Sunnah: What That Day Is For

Ibn Kathir brings two hadiths recorded by Imam Ahmad to show what is actually taking place across this fifty-thousand-year Day. In the first, narrated by Abu Hurayrah (also recorded by Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i), the Prophet ﷺ describes a man who withheld the Zakah due on his camels, cattle, or sheep: on the Day of Resurrection, those very animals return to him at their healthiest and most numerous, trampling and goring him on a level plain — the last of them passing over him, then the first returning to trample him again, "during a day whose measure will be fifty thousand years" — until judgment is passed between all people and he sees which path is his.

In the second, also from Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ describes a hoarder of wealth who did not pay its due: his hoard is heated into plates and used to brand his forehead, side, and back, "until Allah judges between His servants on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years of what you count." Ibn Kathir notes this version was recorded in full by Muslim, though al-Bukhari did not include it.

Both hadiths repeat the same phrase — "a day whose measure is fifty thousand years" — to fix the scale of the reckoning ayah 4 describes: not a poetic flourish, but the actual span across which every person's dealings, down to the Zakah on their livestock, are weighed.

## Living It

The *sa'il's* error was to treat Allah's promise as a bluff to be called. This passage answers not with a description of fire but with a declaration of certainty and scale: coming, unstoppable, from the Lord who owns the very heights, on a Day whose sheer size should sober anyone tempted to mock it. Yet the same fifty-thousand-year Day that overwhelms the arrogant is, in the hadiths, made light for the sincere believer — shorter than a single prayer. The distance between those two experiences of one Day, the sources suggest, is measured by what a person did with far smaller things in this world: an obligation to their Lord, a due paid or withheld.

passages.title: Beautiful patience: they see it far, We see it near
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat form Allah's response to the disbelievers' taunting demand that the punishment they were warned about be brought on immediately. Ayah 5 tells the Prophet ﷺ how to carry that taunting — with "beautiful patience." Ayat 6–7 then explain *why* the taunt was possible in the first place: the disbelievers and the believers are looking at the very same coming reality and seeing something completely different — one sees it as impossibly far off, the other sees it as certain and near.

## The demand that called for patience

Sūrah al-Ma'ārij opens with "A questioner asked concerning a torment about to befall … upon the disbelievers, which none can avert" (ayah 1–2). Ibn Kathir explains that this wording carries an assumed meaning, alluded to by the Arabic letter "Ba" attached to the word for torment: it is as though the questioner was requesting that the coming torment be hastened. Mujahid described this as the disbelievers' own boast, and quoted what the Qur'an records as their words elsewhere: "O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky or bring on us a painful torment" (8:32). Ibn Kathir connects this same demand to Allah's statement in another verse — "And they ask you to hasten on the torment! And Allah fails not His promise" (22:47) — meaning that the torment will occur regardless, and there is no avoiding it.

This is the taunting the Prophet ﷺ had to live inside: people demanding, in effect, "if what you say is true, bring the punishment now." Ayah 5 is Allah's instruction for exactly that pressure.

## "So be patient, with a beautiful patience"

فَاصْبِرْ صَبْرًا جَمِيلًا — Ibn Kathir explains this plainly: "be patient, O Muhammad, with your people's rejection and their seeking to hasten the torment since they think it will not occur." The command to patience is not general life-advice; it is patience with a specific insult — being mocked and dared by people who are certain nothing will happen. Allah situates this in a wider pattern in another verse He cites: "Those who believe not therein seek to hasten it, while those believe are fearful of it, and know that it is the very truth" (42:18). Unbelief produces impatience and mockery; faith produces awe and certainty. The Prophet's ﷺ patience in ayah 5 is the believer's posture held under fire.

## They see it far, We see it near

Ayat 6–7 give the reason the mockery happens at all: إِنَّهُمْ يَرَوْنَهُ بَعِيدًا — "they see it (the torment) afar off" — set against وَنَرَاهُ قَرِيبًا — "But We see it (quite) near."

Ibn Kathir is precise about what this means: the disbelievers see the happening of the torment and the establishment of the Hour "as something that is farfetched" — and he adds that the word *ba'īd* ("far") here does not simply mean distant in time, but "that which is impossible to occur." Against that, "We see it (quite) near" means the believers believe that its occurrence is near, even though its time of occurrence is unknown and no one knows when it will be except Allah. As Ibn Kathir puts it, "All of what is approaching then it is near and it will definitely happen." Nearness here is nearness of certainty, not nearness on a calendar.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān makes the same point even more sharply: here "far" and "near" are not about time or distance at all, but about **possibility**. The disbelievers — the pagans — see the occurrence of the Resurrection as impossible, while Allah sees its occurrence as "not only possible, but a certain reality." Two parties look at the same future event — one calls it unreal, the other calls it settled — and the gap between those two judgments is the whole distance between disbelief and faith.

## Living it

The passage does not ask the believer to calculate when the Hour will come — Ibn Kathir is explicit that its time of occurrence is unknown, and no one knows when it will be except Allah. What it asks for is ayah 5's *ṣabr*: to hold steady under mockery from those who treat the promise of Allah as something to dare Him over, without needing to answer their taunt with a timeline of our own. The believer's certainty is not that the Hour is imminent by the calendar, but that it is *settled* — as near as anything guaranteed to happen must be — and that patience carried with that certainty is what Allah calls beautiful.

passages.title: The Day when no friend asks after a friend
passages.tafsir:
# Surah 70:8–14 — "The Day When No Friend Asks After a Friend"

This passage paints the Day of Judgement as a day when two things dissolve at once: the fixed order of creation, and the fixed bonds of human love. The sky melts, the mountains turn to wisps, and — more devastating still — the people who loved each other most in this world become strangers, each too consumed by his own terror to spare a thought for anyone else. The passage then follows one man, "the criminal," as he tries — and fails — to buy his way out of what he sees coming, offering up everyone dearest to him in a widening, and utterly futile, ransom.

## When the sky melts and the mountains fly apart (ayah 8–9)

Ayah 8 says the sky will be **"like Al-Muhl."** Ibn Kathir records that Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata, Sa'id bin Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, As-Suddi, and others all explained this the same way: *like the residue of oil* — spent, dark, and thick. The sky that today looks like a solid, dependable ceiling over creation will, on that Day, be reduced to something used up and sludge-like.

Ayah 9 says the mountains will be **like 'Ihn** — Mujahid, Qatadah, and As-Suddi glossed this as *fluffed wool*. Ibn Kathir notes this is the same image used elsewhere in the Qur'an of mountains becoming "like carded wool" (101:5). The two things human beings normally treat as permanent — sky above, mountains below — are shown collapsing into their softest, most fragile forms. If even the sky and the mountains, the very furniture of a stable world, cannot hold their form on that Day, nothing that people currently lean on for security will hold either.

## "Though they shall be made to see one another" (ayah 10–11)

Ayah 10 delivers the passage's emotional center: **"no close friend will ask about his friend."** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains the word used here, *hamim*, means specifically a "sincere friend" — not a mere acquaintance, but someone bound to you by real intimacy. The choice of this word makes the point sharper: this is not strangers ignoring strangers. It is a person's closest, most devoted friend, standing right there, and not even asking how he is.

Ayah 11 then adds the detail that makes this so painful: **"though they shall be made to see one another."** Ibn Kathir is explicit that this rules out the excuse of simply not noticing — the close friend sees his companion "in the worst of conditions" and still says nothing, because "he will be worried about himself and will not be able to think of others." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān makes the same point from the other direction: this is *not* because people are physically unable to see each other. "The Divine power, in fact, will make them see each other." The seeing is deliberate, engineered by Allah — the silence that follows is what reveals the true state of a human being when every worldly attachment burns away and only his own fate is left. As Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān puts it, "every person will be in a state of 'each for himself.'"

Ibn Kathir preserves a report from Al-'Awfi, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: people will recognize and be acquainted with each other on that Day — and then flee from each other anyway, once recognized. Recognition does not produce compassion; it produces flight, because — as Allah says elsewhere, which Ibn Kathir quotes here — *"Every man that Day will have enough to make him careless of others"* (80:37).

## The company this ayah keeps

Ibn Kathir draws together several other Qur'anic passages that describe this same collapse of family and kinship on the Last Day, showing that this is not an isolated image but a recurring Qur'anic theme:

- *"O mankind! Have taqwa of your Lord, and fear a Day when no father can avail aught for his son, and nor a son avail aught for his father"* (31:33)
- *"And if one heavily laden calls another to bear his load, nothing of it will be lifted, even though he be near of kin"* (35:18)
- *"When the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask of one another"* (23:101)
- *"That Day shall a man flee from his brother, and from his mother and his father, and from his wife and his children"* (80:34–37)

Placed side by side, these ayat make a single point from several angles: whatever protection kinship, marriage, or friendship gave a person in this world, none of it transfers to the Day of Judgement. Every relationship that exists in this life exists for this life.

## The ransom that cannot be paid (ayah 11–14, and the answer that follows)

The scene then narrows to one figure the Qur'an calls **al-mujrim**, "the criminal." Ibn Kathir explains that he **"would desire ... to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day."** And the list of what he offers grows in a deliberate sequence, each item more precious and more total than the last:

- his children (ayah 11)
- his wife and his brother (ayah 12)
- **his Fasilah who sheltered him** (ayah 13)
- and finally, everyone on earth, all together (ayah 14)

On the word **Fasilah**, Ibn Kathir preserves several explanations from the early scholars, presented as differing views rather than one settled meaning: Mujahid and As-Suddi said it means "his tribe and his kin"; 'Ikrimah said it refers to "the subdivision of his tribe that he is from"; and Ashhab reported from Malik that "his Fasilah is his mother." Whichever reading is taken, the word points to the people whose role in his life was to shelter and protect him — his innermost circle of belonging.

Ibn Kathir comments on the weight of this offer: even the man's own child, "dearer to him than the last beat of his heart in the life of this world," is something he would wish to use as a ransom once he sees the horrors of that Day. And it does not stop there — the list escalates until it reaches the impossible extreme: **everyone on earth**, every last human being, all offered up at once "so that it might save him" (ayah 14).

The Qur'an's answer arrives immediately, in the single word that opens the next ayah: **Kalla** — "By no means!" Ibn Kathir's commentary treats this word as the direct answer to the ransom sequence just described, so it belongs here as the passage's climax, even though the verse numbering places it at the start of ayah 15. Ibn Kathir explains what it closes off: no ransom will be accepted from him, not the whole of mankind, not the greatest wealth that could be found, "even if it was enough gold to fill the entire earth." The child he loved beyond his own heartbeat "would not be accepted from him" either. The escalating list is not meant to describe a real negotiation — there is no bargaining counter on the Day of Judgement — it is meant to show, by exhausting every possible thing a person could offer, that nothing offered will work. The very completeness of the failed offer (children, spouse, sibling, tribe, all mankind) is what proves the point: this Day answers to nothing but what a person actually did.

## What this passage asks of the reader

Earlier in this surah, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains, the pagans "see [the Resurrection] far off" — not distant in time or place, but dismissed by them as impossible to occur — while Allah "sees it near," not only possible but a certain reality (ayat 6–7). Set against that opening, this passage answers with concrete, sensory detail. It is not abstract theology; it is a scene — melting sky, wisping mountains, a friend who will not speak, a man frantically offering up everyone he has ever loved.

The passage does not moralize directly, but its shape carries its own lesson: everything a person in this life is tempted to treat as an ultimate safety net — wealth, children, marriage, tribe, sheer numbers of allies — is shown here reaching its absolute limit. None of it can be exchanged for salvation on that Day. What is being described is not cruelty but consequence: a Day in which only what a person actually believed and actually did stands as currency, and every other currency — however precious it feels now — proves worthless.

passages.title: The Flame that calls the hoarders of wealth
passages.tafsir:
# Surah 70:15–18 — The Flame that Calls the Hoarders of Wealth

## What holds these ayat together

The verses just before this passage describe a scene of pure desperation: on the Day of Judgement, the guilty person (*al-mujrim*) sees the horror ahead of him and wishes he could ransom himself — buying his way out of the punishment with his own children, his wife, his brother, the kinsmen who sheltered him, even everyone on earth (ayat 11–14). Ayah 15 opens with **كَلَّا — "By no means!"** — Allah's flat refusal of that wish. No ransom will be taken, not even if it were the whole earth's gold.

That refusal is not just a "no." It is followed immediately by a description of exactly what this person is facing and exactly who it is coming for. Ayat 15–16 describe the Fire itself — violent enough to strip a person's skin away. Ayat 17–18 describe the Fire as almost alive, actively calling out for two things that mark the people it summons: turning away from the truth, and hoarding wealth without giving Allah His due in it. The four ayat move together as one thought: *no ransom will be accepted — because this is what awaits, and it is specifically calling those who turned away and clung to their money.*

## "By no means! It is truly a raging Flame" (ayah 15)

The pronoun in **إِنَّهَا** ("it") refers to the Fire, and the word **لَظَىٰ (laza)** means "the flaming fire," as Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains. Ibn Kathir notes that after the criminal's vain hope of ransom, Allah is here "describing the Hell-fire and the severity of its heat" — the *kalla* is not an abstract refusal; it is backed up immediately by naming exactly what stands in front of him.

## "Stripping away the scalp" (ayah 16)

**نَزَّاعَةً لِّلشَّوَىٰ** — the Fire is described as *nazza'ah* toward *ash-shawa*. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains that *shawa* is the plural of *shawah*, meaning the scalp or skin of the head, and also the skin of the hands and legs — the outer, visible parts of the body — and describes the phrase as picturing the Fire of Hell as "a raging blaze that will pull out the skin of the scalp."

What is striking in Ibn Kathir's commentary is how many of the early scholars weighed in on exactly what this destruction reaches, each adding a layer:
- **Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid** said it is simply "the skin of the head."
- **Al-Hasan al-Basri and Thabit al-Bunani** said it means "the respectable parts of the face."
- **Qatadah** widened it further: "removing his important organs, and the respectable parts of his face, his creation and his limbs."
- **Ad-Dahhak** described it even more starkly: "it will scrape the flesh and the skin off of the bone until it leaves nothing of it remaining."
- **Ibn Zayd** took *shawa* to mean the marrow of the bones itself, and understood *nazza'ah* as "cutting their bones and transformation of their skins and their form."

Taken together, these scholarly voices are not contradicting each other so much as circling the same reality from different angles — a fire whose violence reaches from the outermost skin down to the very bone and marrow. There is no need to press these differing descriptions into a single technical picture; the Qur'an's own language is doing the work of making the punishment felt, and the scholars are drawing out what that feeling contains.

## "Calling whoever turned their back and turned away" (ayah 17)

Here the passage takes an arresting turn: the Fire does not simply wait to receive people — it **calls** them. Ibn Kathir explains this vividly: "the Fire will call out to its children whom Allah created for it, determining that they will perform the deeds deserving of it in the worldly life. So it will call them on the Day of Judgement with an eloquent and articulate tongue. Then it will pick them out from the people of the gathering just as birds pick seeds."

That image — the Fire singling people out of a vast crowd the way a bird picks out particular seeds — captures something the passage wants us to feel: no one on that Day is lost in the crowd. The Fire that their own deeds shaped comes for them specifically.

Who does it call? Those who **"turned their backs and turned away"** (أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ). Ibn Kathir explains what this turning-away actually consisted of: "they denied with their hearts and abandoned the performance of deeds with their limbs." It is a description of unbelief with two parts — an inner rejection and an outer abandonment: belief that never became conviction in the heart, and conviction that never became action in the limbs.

## "And gathered and hoarded" (ayah 18)

The second thing the Fire calls out for is named in ayah 18: **جَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ** — "he gathered wealth piling it up, and he concealed it." Ibn Kathir is specific about what this concealment means: the person "hid it and refused to give the obligatory right of Allah that was due on it of spending and paying the Zakah." This is not a condemnation of wealth itself, but of wealth kept back from what Allah made obligatory upon it.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān sharpens this into two distinct faults bound together in one phrase: **"accumulated wealth"** points to wealth gathered by unlawful means, while **"hoarded it"** points to the separate failure of "not fulfilling the pecuniary obligations as imposed by the Shariʿah" — meaning Zakah and the other financial duties Allah placed on wealth. The source notes this understanding is "confirmed by authentic ahadith," even where it does not name the specific collections.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir records that concerning this concealment of wealth, "it has been recorded in a Hadith that the Prophet ﷺ said: *'Do not hold back (your wealth), or else Allah will hold back from you'* (لَا تُوعِي فَيُوعِيَ اللهُ عَلَيْكِ)." The wording of the ayah and the wording of this teaching from the Prophet ﷺ share the very same root — *awʿa*, to hold back or hoard — making explicit the link between what the Fire calls out for and what the Prophet ﷺ warned against.

## Living it

The passage moves from the impossible wish of ayah 14 — trying to buy one's way out with children, spouse, and kin — to the plain reason it cannot work: this is a Fire whose reach, in the scholars' words, goes from skin to bone and marrow, and it is actively summoning two kinds of people — those whose hearts never truly submitted and whose limbs never acted on it, and those who gathered wealth and clenched their fist around it rather than giving Allah His due. The remedy the passage points toward, by naming the fault so precisely, is its opposite: a heart that affirms and limbs that act, and wealth that is held with an open hand rather than a hoarding one — Zakah paid and Allah's right in one's money honored. As the hadith puts it, whatever is held back from Allah, Allah holds back in turn.

passages.title: Human impatience, except the praying and the giving
passages.tafsir:
# Surah al-Ma'arij, Ayat 19–25: Human Impatience, Except the Praying and the Giving

This passage opens a long description of the believer's character (Surah al-Ma'arij continues it well beyond ayah 25), but the unit before us does something specific: it names a flaw built into the human being, then begins listing what rescues a person from it. Ayah 19 gives the diagnosis — man was created *haluʿ*. Ayat 20–21 unpack what that word means in practice. And ayat 22–25 open the "except" — the first two qualities, out of what will become a longer list, that lift a person out of this default state: devotion to prayer, and giving from wealth as a recognized right rather than as charity one might withhold. The title "human impatience, except the praying and the giving" captures exactly this movement from diagnosis to exception.

## The word that names it: haluʿ

Ayah 19 declares: *inna al-insana khuliqa halu'a* — "Indeed, humankind was created *haluʿ*." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān unpacks this word carefully: literally it means "one who is greedy, impatient, lacking courage." The Companions and early scholars glossed it from different angles: Ibn ʿAbbas said it describes "a person who is greedy about unlawful wealth"; Saʿid ibn Jubayr said it means "a miserly person"; Muqatil said it means "a person who is impatient and miserly." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes that these are not competing definitions but near-synonyms — the single word *haluʿ* comprehends all of them at once: impatience, greed, and stinginess bundled into one trait. Ibn Kathir reads the ayah the same way, saying Allah is "informing about man and his inclination to corrupt his behavior." The two ayat that follow (20–21) are, in effect, Allah's own commentary on what *haluʿ* looks like when it plays out.

## Why blame a nature?

Before moving on, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān raises and answers an objection that the ayah itself invites: if man is *created* this way — if impatience and stinginess are simply his nature — how can he be blamed for it? This is not a minor aside; it goes to the heart of how the whole passage should be read.

The answer given is that Allah created human nature with the *capacity* for both good and evil, not fixed irreversibly toward evil. Alongside that raw nature, Allah gave man intellect and intelligence, raised Prophets with His message, and sent down Books that state clearly the consequences of every choice a person makes. Man therefore has the ability to choose between good and bad. On this understanding, a person is judged "guilty" — and consequently punished — for *freely choosing* the wrong deed, not for the inborn capacity itself. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān points out that the verses which follow confirm this reading, because they speak only of actions that are matters of choice. Within this very passage, that holds directly: prayer and giving — the two qualities ayat 22–25 go on to describe — are precisely actions of will, not things forced upon a person. The exception clause beginning at ayah 22 is, in other words, proof that the flaw named in ayah 19 is meant to be *overcome*, not excused.

## The two faces of impatience

Ayat 20–21 give the anatomy of *haluʿ* in two mirrored clauses:

*Idha massahu ash-sharru jazuʿa* — "distressed when touched with evil" (20)
*Wa idha massahu al-khayru manuʿa* — "and withholding when touched with good" (21)

Ibn Kathir explains the first half: whenever harm touches such a person, he becomes frightful, worried, and completely overwhelmed — not merely by the severity of the calamity itself, but by his own despair that no good will ever reach him again afterward. It is a collapse of hope, not just a moment of grief.

The second half is the mirror image. When blessing comes to this same person, he becomes stingy with it — he does not share it with others, and he withholds from it the right that Allah has placed within it. Neither state moves him toward Allah — one drives him to despair, the other to hoarding.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān calls this "the fickle nature of man": bad things bring desperation and loss of patience; good things — wealth, comfort — bring begrudging miserliness in spending for good causes. It defines the two key terms precisely for this context: "impatience" here means *that which is outside the limits of the Shariah*, and "niggard" (withholding) means *failing to fulfill the pecuniary obligations the Shariah imposes*. This is an important clarification — the fault being described is not simply feeling afraid or feeling reluctant to spend; it is *acting* outside what Allah has set as the proper bounds of grief and of generosity.

**From the Sunnah.** The bundle records that Imam Ahmad narrated, through a chain reaching Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Sharru ma fi rajulin: shuḥḥun haliʿun wa jubnun khaliʿ"* — "The worst thing that can be in a man is greedy impatience and unrestrained cowardice." This hadith was recorded by Abu Dawud. It names the very same root, *haliʿ*, that Allah uses in ayah 19 to describe the human default — reinforcing that this is a trait to be actively fought, not passively accepted as one's excuse.

## The exception begins: those devoted to prayer

Ayah 22 turns the passage: *illa al-musallin* — "except those who pray." Ibn Kathir explains the force of this exception precisely: the blameworthy description of ayat 19–21 applies to man in general, *except* for the one whom Allah protects, helps, and guides to good, making the means of that good easy for him. Those people are identified here as "those who perform Salah." The choice of description is telling — out of everything a believer might be praised for, the passage singles out prayer as the marker of the person who has escaped the *haluʿ* nature. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws this out further: referring to believers as "the performers of salah" signals that prayer is the greatest sign and the essential characteristic of a believer — in a real sense, the only people who deserve the name "believer" are the people who pray.

## Constant in their prayer

Ayah 23 immediately specifies what kind of prayer rescues a person: *alladhina hum ʿala salatihim da'imun* — "those who consistently perform their prayers." The commentators bring out several layers packed into that one word, *da'imun* ("constant" / "consistent").

**Guarding its times and obligations.** Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, and Ibrahim an-Nakha'i understood this to mean guarding the prayer's proper times and its obligatory elements — praying it correctly and on time, without neglect.

**Tranquility and humble concentration.** ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir understood it instead as stillness and humility (*khushu'*) within the prayer itself, comparing it to Allah's description of the successful believers in Surah al-Mu'minun: "Those who with their Salah are Khashi'un" (23:1–2). Ibn Kathir develops this reading through the very root of the word: *da'im* is the same term used for standing, still water (*al-ma' ad-da'im*). This, he says, proves the obligation of tranquility in prayer — of holding stillness in one's bowing and prostration. The person who rushes through these positions without settling into them is not being "constant" (*da'im*) in his prayer at all; rather, he "pecks in it like the pecking of a crow," and such a person, Ibn Kathir states plainly, is not successful in his prayer.

**Constancy of the deed itself.** A further reading takes *da'imun* to mean maintaining the deed consistently over time, without abandoning it. The bundle records a hadith on the authority of ʿA'ishah, related in the Sahih, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Aḥabbu al-aʿmali ila Allahi adwamuha wa in qall"* — "The most beloved deeds to Allah are those that are most consistent, even if they are few." Steady, small, unbroken devotion outweighs an occasional burst of intensity.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān adds a narration through Imam Baghawi, on the authority of Abu'l-Khayr, in which ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir was asked directly whether "*da'imun*" means praying constantly, without any break, all the time. He answered that this is not the meaning; rather, it means that from the opening of the prayer to its end, a person performs it with due concentration, without any intentional deviation of the heart.

## The recognized right in wealth

Ayat 24–25 give the second exception named in this unit: *wa'lladhina fi amwalihim haqqun maʿlum, li's-sa'ili wa'l-maḥrum* — "and who give the rightful share of their wealth... to the beggar and the poor." Ibn Kathir explains this simply: in the wealth of such people there is a determined, fixed portion set aside for those who are in need.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws out a significant legal point from the phrase *ḥaqqun maʿlum* — "a *known*, specified right," not a vague or optional kindness. This wording shows that the quantifications of Zakah — its rates and its threshold (*niṣab*, the minimum wealth on which it becomes due) — were fixed by Allah Himself, with the details recorded in authentic hadith. Because Allah fixed these measures, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān states, they cannot be altered by anyone, at any time. The word *ḥaqq* — "right" — is doing real work here: this share in one's wealth belongs to the needy as a matter of entitlement, not as a favor the wealthy person is free to grant or withhold at will. That is precisely the opposite of the *manuʿ* — the "withholding" — described back in ayah 21. The one who was described as clutching a blessing and refusing to share it has, in the believer described here, given way to someone who recognizes that a portion of what he holds was never fully his to keep.

The two recipients named — *as-sa'il* ("the one who asks") and *al-maḥrum* ("the deprived") — round out the picture: Ibn Kathir explains that the determined portion in a believer's wealth reaches both the person who asks for help and the person who is simply deprived.

## Living it

Read together, ayat 19–25 draw a straight line: a person is not condemned for the *haluʿ* wired into human nature — panic under loss, tight-fistedness under gain — but for staying there when Allah has shown the way out and given the capacity to take it. The way out named in this passage has two concrete shapes. The first is prayer performed with genuine stillness and humility, not rushed through, and maintained steadily rather than kept up only in bursts — the "most beloved deeds," as the hadith on ʿA'ishah's authority puts it, being those "most consistent, even if they are few." The second is treating a portion of one's wealth not as one's own discretionary generosity but as a right that already belongs to someone else — the one who asks for it and the one who is simply deprived. Fear in hardship and grip in plenty are the default; settled prayer and open-handed giving, as this passage frames them, are what a person becomes when guided out of that default.

passages.title: They hold the Day true and fear a punishment no one is safe from
passages.tafsir:
# Surah 70 (al-Ma'arij), Ayat 26–28

**70:26** — "and who ˹firmly˺ believe in the Day of Judgment;"
**70:27** — "and those who fear the punishment of their Lord—"
**70:28** — "˹knowing that˺ none should feel secure from their Lord's punishment—"

These three ayat are treated as one connected passage: they hold the Day true, and they fear a punishment no one is safe from. A settled certainty about the Day of Judgment (26) produces a living fear of Allah's punishment (27), and ayah 28 explains why that fear is justified — no one is safe from it except by Allah's own security. Ibn Kathir ties the first two together directly: because the believers "are sure of the Final Return (to Allah), the Reckoning and the Recompense," they "perform the deeds of one who hopes for the reward and fears the punishment."

## Where this sits in the passage

These three ayat belong to a longer list describing the qualities of "those who are devoted to Salah" (22) — those Allah exempts from a default human tendency described just before: man was "created very impatient" (19), "apprehensive when evil touches him" (20), and "suppressive when good touches him" (21). Ibn Kathir explains that last trait as someone who, given a blessing, "is stingy with it, not sharing it with others," and so "will withhold the right of Allah with that blessing."

Against that backdrop, the devoted worshippers are described quality by quality: constancy in their prayer (22–23), a recognized share of their wealth for those in need (24–25), and then our three ayat — belief in the Day of Recompense, fear of the punishment, and the knowledge that none is secure from it. The list continues afterward with guarded chastity (29–31), honored trusts and covenants (32), truthful testimony (33), and maintained prayer once more (34), closing with the reward: "Such shall dwell in the Gardens, honored" (35).

Ibn Kathir notes that "Allah begins this discussion (of the believers' attributes) with prayer and He concludes it with prayer," which he says "proves the importance of it and the praise of its noble status." He adds that this is "exactly the same discussion" as what precedes at the beginning of Surat al-Mu'minun (23:1–11), quoting there: "These are indeed the inheritors. Who shall inherit the Firdaws (Paradise). They shall dwell therein forever" (23:10–11).

## The language: three words, three depths

**يُصَدِّقُونَ (yuṣaddiqūn) — "firmly believe."** Ibn Kathir explains that this means the believers "are sure of the Final Return (to Allah), the Reckoning and the Recompense." He draws out the consequence directly: "Therefore, they perform the deeds of one who hopes for the reward and fears the punishment." Belief in the Day, as he presents it, is what produces everything described after it.

**مُشْفِقُونَ (mushfiqūn) — "fear."** Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: "they are fearful and dreadful."

**غَيْرُ مَأْمُونٍ (ghayru ma'mūn) — "none should feel secure."** Ibn Kathir explains: "no one is safe from it (Allah's torment) of those who understand the command from Allah, except by the security of Allah Himself." Security from the punishment is not something a person secures for himself — it is granted by Allah alone.

## What the scholars draw from this

Ibn Kathir's own summary — that the believers "perform the deeds of one who hopes for the reward and fears the punishment" — is the thread that ties these three ayat together: certainty about the Day produces both hope and fear, and it is the fear side of that pairing that ayat 27 and 28 dwell on. His closing note on ayah 28 sets the boundary carefully: safety from Allah's punishment belongs to no one "except by the security of Allah Himself" — it is not something granted by a person's own confidence in his deeds, however devoted those deeds may be.

Ibn Kathir also draws attention to how prayer frames this entire list, opening it (22–23) and closing it (34), which he says "proves the importance of it and the praise of its noble status" — the same pattern, he notes, as the opening of Surat al-Mu'minun. Our ayat sit inside that framed list, describing the inward certainty and fear that Ibn Kathir says produce the outward "deeds of one who hopes for the reward and fears the punishment."

## Living it

What these three ayat ask of the reader is not abstract. Belief in the Day of Recompense (26) is meant to be real enough to produce genuine fear (27) — the "fearful and dreadful" watchfulness Ibn Kathir describes. And ayah 28 closes off any shortcut: safety from Allah's punishment is not something a person's own confidence in his good deeds can secure for him. As Ibn Kathir puts it, it comes only "by the security of Allah Himself" — something sought and hoped for, never assumed.

passages.title: Guarded chastity, kept trusts, upright testimony — then the Gardens
passages.tafsir:
This passage completes a portrait that Surah Al-Ma'arij has been building since it described man's natural impatience — restless when harm touches him, tight-fisted when good touches him (as the surah says a few ayat earlier). Against that default human weakness, the surah lists the qualities Allah has carved into those He guides. Ayat 29–35 give the last three of those qualities and then the reward that crowns them all: guarded chastity, faithful trusteeship, and honest testimony — bookended by devotion to prayer — leading into the Gardens, "honored" (ayah 35). What holds the unit together is a single logic: purity of the body, honesty in what is entrusted to you, and truthfulness in what you say are three different tests of the same thing — whether a person can be relied upon, by Allah and by other people, in matters no one is forcing them to get right.

## Guarding chastity, and where the line is drawn (29–31)

Ayah 29 says believers are "those who guard their chastity" — literally, their private parts (*furuj*). Ibn Kathir explains this as keeping the private parts away from everything forbidden, and not placing them anywhere except where Allah has permitted. Ayah 30 then draws the boundary precisely: this guarding is relaxed only "with their wives or those in their rightful possession" — Ibn Kathir specifies this refers to female slaves lawfully owned — "for then they are not blameworthy." Ayah 31 closes the door firmly on everything else: "whoever seeks beyond that are the transgressors" (*al-'adun*).

Maʿārif ul-Qur'an draws out what "beyond that" excludes. It rules out any woman who falls, according to the Shari'ah, within the prohibited degrees of relation. And it specifically names *mut'ah* (a temporary hired arrangement for sexual enjoyment) as falling outside the permission too, since it is not a marriage according to the Shari'ah and is therefore swept into the meaning of "seeking beyond that."

Ibn Kathir notes that the fuller explanation of this passage was already given at the opening of Surat Al-Mu'minun, so it isn't repeated in detail here.

**On private acts beyond even this.** Maʿārif ul-Qur'an records that most jurists take ayah 31's generality to also forbid masturbation, since it is a use of the private parts outside the two permitted channels named in ayah 30. Ibn Juraij asked Sayyidna 'Ata' about it, who called it *makruh* (reprehensible) and added that he had heard that on the Plain of Gathering some people will come with their hands "pregnant" — people, he felt, who used to satisfy their desire with their own hands. Sayyidna Sa'id ibn Jubair said that Allah punished a nation who used to fondle their private parts with their hands this way. A hadith states that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Cursed is he who marries his hand" — but Maʿārif ul-Qur'an is careful to note, citing Mazhari, that the chain of authorities for this particular hadith is weak. It's worth being honest about that grading rather than repeating the wording as if it were firmly established; the stronger basis for the ruling, according to the jurists cited, is the general sense of ayah 31 itself.

The shape of these three ayat together is worth sitting with: chastity in Islam is not presented as suppression of desire but as its channeling. Ayah 30 doesn't shame desire — it locates it, inside marriage and lawful possession. Ayah 31 then says: anyone who won't accept that boundary, and goes looking past it, has stepped into transgression. Guarding the private parts, in other words, is really about a person's willingness to accept a limit Allah has set on something intensely personal — which is exactly why it belongs on this list of tests of reliability.

## Keeping trusts and covenants (32)

Ayah 32 moves from the body to obligations owed to others: "those who are true to their trusts (*amanat*) and their covenant (*'ahd*)." Maʿārif ul-Qur'an makes a point of the grammar here: *amanat* is the plural of *amanah*, the same word used in ayah 4:58, "Surely, Allah commands you to fulfill trust obligations towards those entitled to them." Because the Qur'an uses the plural, the meaning widens far beyond "an item someone deposited with you for safekeeping." It reaches every obligatory right a person owes and must fulfill — the rights Allah has over a person (salah, fasting, hajj, zakah, all classed here as *amanat*) together with the rights human beings have over one another, including contracts and covenants people freely enter into with each other. Maʿārif ul-Qur'an is blunt about the stakes: breach of trusts and covenants is, in essence, dishonesty — and fulfilling the terms one has agreed to is obligatory, so failing to comply amounts to a betrayal of trust.

Ibn Kathir frames this ayah as the direct opposite of a hypocrite's character, citing what is reported in an authentic hadith: "The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks his promise, and when he is entrusted he betrays." A related wording is also given: "When he speaks he lies, when he makes a covenant he breaks it, and when he argues he is abusive." Read against ayah 32, the point is sharp — trustworthiness and truthful covenant-keeping are not minor social virtues; the Qur'an and this hadith both treat their absence as one of the defining marks of hypocrisy.

## Standing firm in testimony (33)

Ayah 33 adds a third test: "those who are honest in their testimony" (*shahadat*). Maʿārif ul-Qur'an again draws meaning from the plural — *shahadat* is the plural of *shahadah*, and the plural signals that there are many categories of testimony a believer must be upright and firm in, not one narrow legal context. The commentary lists what falls under this: testifying to the faith of Islam itself, to Allah's existence and His Oneness, and to Muhammad ﷺ as His Final Messenger; the obligation to testify to having sighted the crescent moon of Ramadan; giving a true and accurate account as an expert witness in Shari'ah matters and in judicial hearings generally; and the duty to come forward and testify when one is summoned. It is prohibited, the commentary adds, to add to or omit any part of what one testifies to.

Ibn Kathir makes the same point about completeness: standing firm in testimony means guarding it — neither adding to it nor subtracting from it, nor concealing it when it should be given. He connects this to Allah's warning elsewhere in the Qur'an, "whoever hides it [testimony], surely his heart is sinful" (2:283). Testimony, on this reading, is truthfulness under a kind of social pressure — the pressure to soften, inflate, or simply stay silent — and the believer is the one who resists all three temptations.

## Prayer, again, at the close of the list (34)

Ayah 34 returns to where this description of the believer began: "those who are properly observant of their prayers" — using the verb *yuhafizun*, "they guard/maintain." Ibn Kathir explains this as maintaining prayer's proper times, its pillars, its obligatory elements, and its recommended acts. He draws attention to something structural: this whole description of the believer's character opens with prayer and closes with prayer, which he reads as proof of prayer's importance and the nobility of its standing — and he notes that this is exactly the same pattern found at the beginning of Surat Al-Mu'minun.

## The reward: Gardens, and honored (35)

The list ends in ayah 35: "these will be in Gardens, held in honour." Ibn Kathir reads "honored" (*mukramun*) as meaning they will be honored with every kind of pleasure and delight. He also points again to the parallel with Al-Mu'minun, where the same list of qualities concludes, "These are indeed the inheritors, who will inherit al-Firdaws; they will abide therein forever" (23:10–11). Here in Al-Ma'arij, the conclusion is phrased differently but carries the same weight: a place of honor, not merely of escape from punishment.

## Reading the passage as a whole

Step back from the individual ayat and the shape of the passage becomes clear. Man, left to his own impatient nature, grabs when he can and withholds when he can — that was the surah's opening diagnosis. Everything from there is Allah describing what it looks like when a person is instead shaped by devotion to Him. Ayat 29–31 test whether that shaping reaches the most private and hardest-to-police area of a person's life — desire itself. Ayah 32 tests whether it reaches what other people have placed in their hands, whether literal deposits or the far wider category of divine and human obligations owed. Ayah 33 tests whether it reaches what comes out of their mouth when the truth is inconvenient. And ayah 34 returns, deliberately, to prayer — the discipline that Ibn Kathir notes both opens and closes the whole list — as if to say that all of this integrity, in body, in trust, and in speech, is sustained by the standing relationship with Allah that prayer maintains. The reward named in ayah 35 is not a bare escape from Hell but honor — dwelling as guests treated with dignity, because in this life they treated what Allah entrusted to them, and what people entrusted to them, with the same care.

passages.title: Why do the deniers rush hoping for Paradise?
passages.tafsir:
## Rushing Toward You, Then Peeling Away

This short passage (ayat 36–39) paints one vivid scene and then delivers one devastating argument. The scene: disbelievers crowd toward the Prophet ﷺ, then break off to the right and the left into little scoffing circles. The argument: these same people still somehow hope to enter Paradise — yet they can't even accept the plain evidence of their own beginnings. What holds the unit together is the astonishment in Allah's opening question, "So what is the matter with them?" — the sheer incongruity of people who reject the Hereafter while still, absurdly, hoping for its best reward.

**The setting.** Ibn Kathir explains that this is Allah rebuking the disbelievers of the Prophet's ﷺ own time. They had seen him. They had seen the guidance Allah sent through him and the "magnificent miracles" Allah supported him with. And after all of that, they still fled from him and cut themselves off from him. Ibn Kathir draws out the parallel to another verse describing the same posture: "Then what is wrong with them that they run away from admonition? As if they were frightened wild donkeys, fleeing from a beast of prey" (74:49–51). It's a startling image — people bolting not from danger but from truth itself, as if the message were the predator and ignorance the safety. "This Ayah is similar," Ibn Kathir says of our passage: the same fright, the same flight, now aimed at the Messenger ﷺ himself.

## "Rushing" — Toward Him, Then Away From Him

Ayah 36 asks: *"So what is the matter with the disbelievers that they rush headlong (muhtiʿīn) before you"* — meaning before the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir glosses this as, "what is wrong with these disbelievers who are with you, O Muhammad? Why are they *muhtiʿīn* — hastily running away from you?" Al-Hasan al-Basri is cited for the same sense: "*Muhtiʿīn* means departing."

But there's a second layer to the word that Ibn ʿAbbas brings out (as reported by al-ʿAwfi): "They are looking in your direction." Put the two together and you get the full, almost comic-tragic picture: they crane their necks toward the Prophet ﷺ — staring, curious, unable to look away — and then, rather than let that gaze lead them to the truth, they wheel off into their own little factions to mock what they've just heard.

## Little Circles of Scorn

That wheeling-away is what ayah 37 names directly: *"from the right and the left, in groups (ʿizīn)."* Ibn Kathir explains that the singular of *ʿizīn* is *ʿizah*, from a root meaning "separating" — so the word itself pictures a crowd splintering into distinct little knots rather than standing together. Ibn ʿAbbas's comment on this ayah makes the tone unmistakable: *"Al-ʿIzīn* is a group among the people. 'On the right and on the left' means they are turning away — right and left — from him [the Prophet ﷺ] and mocking him." This isn't neutral crowd behavior; it is organized derision, huddles of scoffers peeling off from the main gathering.

Ibn Kathir supports the sense of the word with a hadith: Jabir bin Samurah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out to them while they were sitting in circles, and he said, *"Mā liya arākum ʿizīn"* — "Why do I see you all in groups?" This hadith is recorded, as the source states, by Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, an-Nasaʾi, and Ibn Jarir. Ibn Kathir brings it in simply to anchor the meaning of the word *ʿizīn* — scattered clusters rather than one united body — which is exactly the picture ayah 37 draws of the deniers around the Prophet ﷺ: not one confused crowd, but many separate pockets of mockery.

## Hoping for a Paradise They Are Fleeing From

Then comes the rebuke that gives the passage its edge. Ayah 38 asks: *"Does every one of them hope to be admitted into a Garden of Delight?"* Ibn Kathir draws out the sheer contradiction packed into this question: "Is this their wish, yet they flee from the Messenger ﷺ in aversion to the truth? Are they hoping that they will be admitted into the Gardens of Delight?" The answer, delivered as the opening word of ayah 39, is *"Kallā"* — "But no!" As Ibn Kathir puts it plainly, their real abode, given how they are behaving, is Hell, not the Garden they claim to hope for.

This is the passage's central irony: people who reject the Messenger ﷺ, mock his message, and deny the Day of Judgment altogether still somehow expect its finest reward. Hope without acceptance, desire without submission — Allah exposes the incoherence of wanting Paradise's fruit while cutting down the tree that bears it.

## The Proof They Already Carry In Themselves

Ayah 39 then turns from rebuke to argument. Having denied the Final Abode as something "farfetched," the deniers are answered with evidence drawn from nothing more exotic than their own origin: *"Indeed, We created them out of that which they [already] know."* Ibn Kathir explains this means they were created "from despised semen" — a lowly, unremarkable fluid, and one whose nature they already fully know, since it is common to every human being. The Qurʾan makes the same point elsewhere, cited here by Ibn Kathir as a parallel: *"Did We not create you from a despised water?"* (77:20), and in fuller detail: *"So let man see from what he is created! He is created from a water gushing forth, proceeding from between the backbone and the ribs. Verily He is able to bring him back!"* (86:5–10).

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah brings this forward "as a proof against them": the initiation of their creation, and the fact that repeating that process is "something easier than performing it the first time" — a truth, he notes, "that they themselves confess to." Allah brought a human being into existence from something as unremarkable — even, in Ibn Kathir's word, "despised" — as this fluid. If that first creation was within Allah's power, then bringing the same person back after death, which is only a repetition, is no harder. The disbelievers are not being asked to imagine some abstract, unfamiliar power; they are being pointed to a fact about their own bodies that they cannot deny, because "they already know" it. Their denial of resurrection collapses under the weight of a truth they carry within themselves.

## What This Asks of the Reader

Taken as a whole, these four ayat hold up a mirror to two failures at once. The first is social and moral: turning revelation into a spectacle to gawk at and then mock in cliques, rather than letting it change anything. The second is intellectual and spiritual: wanting the reward of faith — Paradise — while refusing the substance of faith, and denying a Hereafter whose plausibility is written into one's own origin. The passage doesn't ask the reader to accept something mysterious on blind trust; it asks only for honesty about what is already known and evident — that the One who began the process of human life is more than capable of completing it by bringing that life back.

passages.title: An oath on resurrection: let them play till their Day
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah 70:40–44 — An Oath on Resurrection: Let Them Play Till Their Day

## What holds this passage together

These five āyāt close Sūrah al-Maʿārij with Allah swearing by the Lord of every point where the sun rises and sets that He is able to resurrect mankind, indeed to remake them in something *better* than what they have now (ayah 40–41). Having settled that, He tells the Prophet ﷺ to simply leave the deniers to their idle talk and games (ayah 42), because a Day is coming when they will burst from their graves in a desperate rush (ayah 43), eyes lowered, disgrace clinging to them (ayah 44). The unit moves from **certainty** (the oath and its proof) to **patience** (leave them) to **vision** (what that Day will actually look like for people who refused to believe in it). It is Allah's final word, in this sūrah, to those who fled from the Prophet ﷺ in mocking little circles (mentioned just before, in āyāt 36–39) while still somehow hoping for Paradise: their own origin — mere fluid they find unremarkable — is already proof that the One who started them can finish them.

## The oath: "I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests"

Ibn Kathīr explains that "the Lord of the easts and the wests" (*mashāriq*, *maghārib* — plural: "easts" and "wests") means the One who created the heavens and the earth and set the east and the west in place — the One who subjects the stars, causing them to appear in the eastern sky and vanish in the western sky. Allah swears by that mastery that "We are able" (*la-qādirūn*) — able to bring people back, and not merely back, but *better* than they were.

There is a grammatical subtlety Ibn Kathīr draws out: the oath opens with a negation — *falā uqsimu*, "so no, I swear." He explains this shows Allah is "swearing by a denial of their claim" — the disbelievers had denied the Final Return, the Reckoning, the Resurrection, the Gathering. The negation at the front of the oath is itself a rebuttal: *no* — it is not as you say. The matter will occur; there is no way of avoiding it.

## The proof behind the oath

Ibn Kathīr situates this as the climax of an argument Allah has been building since ayah 39, where He reminded the disbelievers that He created them "out of that which they know" — meaning from ordinary, unremarkable fluid (semen), the very thing they themselves would call insignificant. The logic: if Allah could originate a human being from something so lowly, repeating that act — bringing the same person back — is, in Ibn Kathīr's words, "something easier than performing it the first time." This is a point the disbelievers themselves implicitly concede, since they do not deny where they came from.

Ibn Kathīr supports this with related verses cited in the tafsīr: that the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, "yet most of mankind know not" (40:57); that Allah, who created the heavens and earth without being wearied by it, is surely able to give life to the dead (46:33); and that the One who created the heavens and earth is able to create their like again, for "His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be!' — and it is" (36:81–82). The disbelievers had already witnessed something more convincing than the Day of Judgement itself — the creation of the heavens and the earth and the subjection of the creatures within them — yet failed to draw the obvious conclusion.

## "To replace them by others better than them" (ayah 41)

Ibn Kathīr's primary reading of *nubaddila khayran minhum* is that on the Day of Judgement Allah will bring people back to life "in bodies that are better than these bodies that they have now" — a re-creation, not a patched-up repetition. And "We are not to be outrun" (*mā naḥnu bi-masbūqīn*) means, in Ibn Kathīr's gloss, simply "We are not unable" — nothing can outstrip or frustrate Allah's power, a point reinforced by verses he cites: "Does man think that We shall not assemble his bones? Yes, We are able to put together in perfect order the tips of his fingers" (75:3–4), and "We have decreed death to you all, and We are not outstripped, to transfigure you and create you in forms that you know not" (56:60–61).

Ibn Kathīr also records that Ibn Jarīr preferred a different reading of the same phrase — that it means "a nation who will obey Us and not disobey Us," i.e., replacing this generation with a more obedient one, comparing it to Allah's statement elsewhere, "And if you turn away, He will exchange you for some other people and they will not be like you" (47:38). Ibn Kathīr notes both views but states his own judgment plainly: "the first interpretation is more obvious, since the other āyāt support that" — meaning the reading about resurrected bodies being made better — while adding the caveat scholars use in genuine disagreement, "Allah the Most High knows best."

## "So leave them to plunge in vain talk and play about" (ayah 42)

Having settled the certainty of the Day, Allah turns to the Prophet ﷺ with a command: *fadharhum* — "so leave them." Ibn Kathīr explains this means leaving them "in their denial, disbelief and obstinance" to *yakhūḍū wa yalʿabū* — "plunge in vain talk and play about." This is not permission for them to disbelieve, nor indifference on Allah's part; it is a statement about strategy and certainty. The outcome no longer needs defending or forcing — "until they meet their Day which they are promised," when, as Ibn Kathīr puts it, "they are going to know the outcome of that and taste its evil consequences." The instruction releases the Prophet ﷺ, and by extension every believer who faces mockery and stubborn denial, from the burden of having to win an argument that time itself will settle.

## The scene of Resurrection (ayah 43): rushing "as if to a Nusub"

Ayah 43 paints the moment itself: *yawma yakhrujūna min al-ajdāthi sirāʿan ka-annahum ilā nuṣubin yūfiḍūn* — "the Day they come out of the graves quickly, as if rushing to a Nuṣub." Ibn Kathīr explains that people will rise from their graves the instant Allah calls them to the place of reckoning, moving as urgently as someone rushing toward some monumental object.

The word itself carries two recorded recitations, and each opens a different layer of meaning — a good example of how a single letter's vowelling changes the picture. Most reciters read it as *Nasb* (fatḥah on the nūn, sukūn on the ṣād), a verbal noun meaning "something erected" — Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk explained it as "a flag"; Abū ʿĀliyah and Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr said, "a goal." On this reading, the image is of people surging toward a visible rallying-point, the way a crowd rushes toward a signal-post. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, however, recited it *Nuṣub* (ḍammah on both letters), meaning an idol. Several other early authorities (Mujāhid, Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, Muslim al-Baṭīn, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Abū Ṣāliḥ, ʿĀṣim ibn Bahdalah, Ibn Zayd, and others) carried this same idol-reading. On that recitation the comparison turns pointed and ironic: their rush toward the resurrection-gathering will resemble how they used to hurry, in worldly life, to reach an idol first — jostling to be the one who touched it before anyone else. Allah is not merely describing speed; He is holding up a mirror to the very eagerness they once wasted on false gods, now spent uselessly rushing toward a Day they denied.

## "Eyes lowered... ignominy covering them" (ayah 44)

The passage closes on the disbelievers' bearing at that Reckoning: *khāshiʿatan abṣāruhum tarhaquhum dhillah* — their eyes humbled, disgrace covering them over, rendered here as "with eyes downcast, utterly covered with disgrace." Ibn Kathīr reads the humiliation as measured recompense: "in return for how they behaved arrogantly in the worldly life by refusing to be obedient to Allah." The very people who, in this life, walked away from the Prophet ﷺ mockingly — described earlier as fleeing "on the right and on the left" in scattered, scoffing circles — will stand that Day with lowered eyes and this disgrace covering them. Then comes the closing line, almost a verdict read aloud: *dhālika al-yawmu alladhī kānū yūʿadūn* — "that is the Day which they were promised." The oath that opened the passage and the scene that closes it meet here: what Allah swore was true, they now see with their own humbled eyes.

## Taking it in

Read as one movement, the passage teaches a particular way of holding certainty about the unseen. It does not ask the believer to argue every mocker into submission; it asks for the confidence Allah models in ayah 42 — state the truth, then let people be, because the Day itself is the final argument. And it grounds that confidence not in guesswork but in something each person can already see: the creation of the heavens and the earth — in Ibn Kathīr's words, something "more convincing than the Day of Judgement" itself — and their own origin from something plain and unremarkable, which they themselves do not deny. Both are already granted by anyone who has eyes to see or breath to deny it.
